planting.note: Start seed indoors under heat eight weeks before the last frost and transplant out once nights stay reliably above 55F, since the slender pods are best picked young and green long before any red color develops.

directions: Piparra, also sold as guindilla de Ibarra, is a thin, pale-green finger pepper traditionally grown around Ibarra in Gipuzkoa in Spain's Basque Country and harvested immature for pickling in vinegar brine. The plants are compact and heavily productive, so pick pods continuously at 3-4 inches long to keep new flowers setting through the season. Pickled piparras are a tapas-bar staple across the Basque Country, served alone threaded on skewers or as the traditional partner to gildas, the anchovy-and-olive pintxo. The mild, tangy pods are rarely eaten fresh raw and are almost always cured rather than cooked.

scientific_name: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Carxofa del Prat'

planting.note: Plant rooted offshoots or crowns into deep, sandy, well-manured soil in early spring; this variety is traditionally grown in the low, humid delta soils of the Llobregat river and resents waterlogging despite needing steady moisture.

directions: Carxofa del Prat is a violet-tinged, tightly furled artichoke landrace grown in the market-garden soils of El Prat de Llobregat near Barcelona and protected under a Catalan geographical indication since the early 2000s. The plants send up multiple smaller, tender buds rather than one dominant head, and growers harvest them young and compact for the prized winter and early-spring crop. Its delicate, slightly sweet flesh with minimal choke makes it a favorite eaten raw, shaved thin into salads, or simply sauteed whole in olive oil as carxofes a la llauna. The crop is closely tied to the reclaimed delta farmland south of Barcelona's airport, one of the last pockets of traditional market gardening in the metropolitan area.
sources: Generalitat de Catalunya DOP/IGP product documentation

planting.note: Along the Catalan coast this pea is traditionally autumn-sown for a late-winter to early-spring harvest in mild maritime soil; in colder climates sow instead as early as the ground can be worked in spring.

directions: Pèsol de Llavaneres is a sweet, tender early garden pea grown along the sandy Maresme coast north of Barcelona, especially around Sant Andreu de Llavaneres, where the mild sea-facing microclimate allows an unusually early winter-into-spring crop. Vines are trained up brush or netting and pods are picked young while still slender for maximum sweetness, since the sugars convert quickly once the peas swell. In Catalan cuisine these peas arrive at the same time of year as calcots and are traditionally sauteed simply with a little ham or served alongside spring lamb. Local growers prize the variety for its tenderness and short shelf life, which has kept it mostly a regional farmers'-market crop rather than a commodity pea.
sources: Generalitat de Catalunya local product registry

planting.note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in dormant season on a dwarfing or semi-vigorous rootstock, since this old variety is an irregular, often lopsided bearer that benefits from a sheltered site and a pollination partner, as it sets fruit unreliably on its own.

directions: Cornish Gilliflower is a strongly ribbed, lopsided dessert apple first noted in a cottage garden near Truro, Cornwall in the early 1800s and later taken up by Victorian nurserymen for its intensely perfumed, almost clove-like aroma. The deep red-flushed, russeted fruit keeps well into winter and develops a rich, dry, aromatic sweetness that many consider one of the most distinctive flavors among English heirloom apples. Trees are vigorous but can be shy and irregular bearers, so growers typically graft it onto a more precocious rootstock and thin crowded fruit to encourage annual cropping. It remains a connoisseur's variety kept alive mainly through National Fruit Collection holdings and specialist heritage orchards rather than commercial production.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in the dormant season in well-drained soil with good air flow, since this variety is prone to scab in damp seasons and benefits from an open, airy site typical of its native Cornish orchards.

directions: Cornish Aromatic is a russeted, orange-flushed dessert apple traced back to a tree found near Truro, Cornwall around the early 1800s, prized for its firm, nutty flesh and distinctive warm, spicy-sweet flavor that intensifies in storage through autumn into early winter. The irregularly ribbed fruit has thick, rough skin that protects it well in the root cellar, making it historically valued as a keeper in an era before refrigeration. It is grown almost exclusively by heritage orchardists and fruit collections today, prized by cider and dessert-apple enthusiasts for its complexity rather than for heavy cropping. The tree is moderately vigorous and best suited to maritime or mild climates similar to its Cornish origin.
